134.title: Angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2)
134.hook: welcome strangers; some have hosted angels without knowing
134.howItsDone: Many Christians practice hospitality by welcoming visitors at church, opening their homes for meals, and hosting travelers; some monasteries keep guesthouses for visitors, following Saint Benedict's rule to receive guests as Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alms without a trumpet, and your line: let it stay secret. Today, the open door.

It's the hottest part of the day. An old man sits in the doorway of his tent. He looks up, and three strangers are standing nearby. He doesn't wait for them to ask. He runs, in that heat. He bows and begs them to stay. He fetches water to wash their feet, tells his wife to bake bread from the good flour, picks out a calf himself. He calls it a little bread. It's a feast. He stands under a tree while they eat. It's Abraham, in Genesis eighteen, and before the day is over he learns who his guests really were. Much later, a letter in the New Testament seems to remember that afternoon.
screen: `THE HOTTEST PART OF THE DAY.` → `THREE STRANGERS.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS.`

segments.voice: Hospitality. The New Testament's Greek word is philoxenia: philo, love; xenos, stranger. Love of the stranger. Not of your friends, which is easy, but of the person you don't know yet. Near its end, the letter to the Hebrews puts it on a short list of how to live. In the King James Bible: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares: without knowing. Readers have long heard Abraham in that line, though the letter never names him. The visitors at his tent turn out to be messengers of God, and in the story one of them promises that old Sarah will have a son. Abraham didn't welcome them because they were angels. He welcomed them, and they turned out to be. In the world of these stories, this was no small courtesy. A traveler far from home depended on someone's open door for food and safety. Opening it could be a lifeline, and it could cost you. In Matthew, Jesus says the king will say at the end: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Saint Benedict, writing a rule for monks, said every guest should be welcomed as Christ, quoting that same line. Jewish tradition treasures the story too: welcoming guests is counted a mitzvah, a commandment, and Abraham's open tent is its picture. The idea is simple, and harder than it sounds: the person at your door might carry more than you can see.
screen: `PHILOXENIA — LOVE OF THE STRANGER.` · `SOME HAVE ENTERTAINED ANGELS.` · `AN OPEN DOOR, A LIFELINE.` · `EVERY GUEST AS CHRIST.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Picture your own door, at home or at work, and the people who come to it that you barely notice: the delivery driver, the new person on the team, the neighbor you've nodded at for two years. Pick one face and imagine offering them something small to drink, water, a coffee, a cold soda. If you pray, ask to see that person clearly; if you don't, simply hold their face a moment with a little more warmth than usual.
Hospitality. In Greek, philoxenia, love of the stranger. Abraham ran to his guests before he knew who they were.
Your line: strangers might be angels. Abraham ran first and learned later. See you tomorrow.

run to them, bow, and beg them to stay and eat.

135.title: The church sings (Colossians 3:16)
135.hook: the first Christians sang psalms, hymns and spiritual songs
135.howItsDone: Nearly every Christian church sings when it gathers: Orthodox and many Catholic services chant much of the liturgy, and Protestant congregations sing hymns and worship songs together, often with an organ, piano or band.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospitality, love of the stranger, and your line: strangers might be angels. Today, the church gathers, and sings.

A birthday. A stadium. A funeral where nobody can quite hold the note. When a room sings together, something happens that doesn't happen when one person talks. You may remember Paul and Silas from day eighty-four, singing in the stocks at Philippi while the prisoners listened. That night wasn't a one-off. Wherever the first Christians turn up, a song is close by. Ever since, in cathedrals, basements and fields, when Christians gather, they sing.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF VOICES.` → `PAUL AND SILAS WEREN'T A ONE-OFF.` → `WHEN THEY GATHER, THEY SING.`

segments.voice: The church sang from its very first night. After the last supper, Mark says, Jesus and his friends sang before walking out: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." Many scholars think it was the psalms Jews sang at Passover, still sung at the Passover table today. So the church's first song was a Jewish song. Then Paul, writing to the Christians in Colossae, describes their gatherings. In the King James Bible: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Nobody knows exactly where one kind ends and the next begins. Psalms likely means the old songs of Israel; hymns, songs of praise; spiritual songs, maybe something newer, even made up in the moment. Notice who teaches whom: one another. Singing was how they taught. A tune carries words into memory in a way a lecture can't. And outsiders noticed. Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor that these odd people called Christians met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god. An official, not a friend, is one of our earliest witnesses that they sang. Today's line, who sings prays twice, is often credited to Saint Augustine, though scholars can't find those exact words in his writings. He did write about weeping when he heard the church sing. It stuck because many recognize it: sing a prayer, and your breath and body pray it too.
screen: `THEY SANG AN HYMN, AND WENT OUT.` · `PSALMS, HYMNS, SPIRITUAL SONGS.` · `SINGING WAS HOW THEY TAUGHT.` · `A ROMAN HEARD THEM BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.`

segments.voice: You don't need a good voice: bring to mind one line of a hymn or church song you know, Amazing grace, Holy, holy, holy, Jesus loves me, or if none come, a tune from a wedding or a funeral. Breathe in and sing or hum it softly, once, then again slower, noticing where the sound sits in your chest. If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if you don't, just notice what a song does to your breath.
Spiritual songs, Paul's third kind of church music, maybe newer, even made up in the moment, alongside psalms and hymns.
Your line: who sings prays twice. A good voice is optional. That's day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: Watts and Wesley
136.hook: two Englishmen wrote thousands of hymns still sung, like When I Survey and And Can It Be
136.howItsDone: Many churches sing hymns by Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley from printed hymnals or screens, especially at Christmas, Easter and funerals, and some Christians read hymns privately as poems or prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, and your line: who sings prays twice. Today, two hymn writers.

An English chapel, and a teenager named Isaac Watts sits in the pews, bored. The churches he knew sang mainly the psalms, set into stiff rhymes, often lined out one line at a time by a leader and dragged back by the congregation. The story goes that young Isaac complained, and his father said, more or less: then write something better. So he did. Hymn after hymn, some still sung at Christmas and on Good Friday. A generation later, a restless Anglican priest named Charles Wesley would write thousands more. Between them, they gave English-speaking congregations a new kind of song.
screen: `A BORED TEENAGER IN CHURCH.` → `THEN WRITE SOMETHING BETTER.` → `HYMN AFTER HYMN.`

segments.voice: Hymn, from the Greek hymnos, a song of praise to a god or a hero. For Christians, it's a song of praise in verses, sung by the whole congregation. Watts did something that sounds simple now and was daring then: new songs in plain English, in the voice of the people singing them, about the gospel. People call him the father of English hymnody. He wrote Joy to the World and O God, Our Help in Ages Past. And in 1707 he published When I Survey the Wondrous Cross. It walks slowly toward the cross, looks, and ends with the line that became today's carry: "Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." It doesn't argue. It just looks and answers. Then Charles Wesley. He and his brother John started the movement that became the Methodists, and Charles wrote hymns by the thousand: Hark! the Herald Angels Sing, Love Divine, All Loves Excelling, and And Can It Be, written around his own conversion in 1738. It's full of astonishment: "Amazing love! How can it be That Thou, my God, shouldst die for me?" One a careful poet, the other a fountain. Watts was a Congregationalist, Wesley an Anglican, and their hymns now turn up in the hymnals of churches neither man belonged to. Both keep landing on the same astonished word: amazing. A hymn is theology you can sing, in words plain enough that a tired congregation can carry it home.
screen: `HYMNOS — A SONG OF PRAISE.` · `WATTS: WHEN I SURVEY, 1707.` · `WESLEY: HYMNS BY THE THOUSAND.` · `THEOLOGY YOU CAN SING.` · then, large: `LOVE SO AMAZING, SO DIVINE.`

segments.voice: Say the last verse of When I Survey slowly, spoken, not sung, with a pause at every comma: "Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small; Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." Sit with it and let one word catch: realm, small, demands. If you pray, pray it back slowly; if you don't, read it as what it is, a man looking at something and finding his hands empty.
Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise. A poem in verses, made for a whole congregation to sing.
Your line: love so amazing. Sung or simply spoken, it still lands just the same. Until tomorrow.

137.title: The spirituals
137.hook: enslaved Africans in America made songs of Moses, Jordan and freedom that carried hope and plans
137.howItsDone: Spirituals are sung in many Black churches and in churches of every kind, by choirs and congregations, and are often sung in services remembering freedom, justice and the civil rights movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Watts, Wesley and the hymn, and your line: love so amazing. Today, songs of people who were not free.

A field in the American South, before the Civil War. The sun is brutal and the work doesn't stop. Enslaved men and women are often forbidden to read or to gather, and can be sold away from their own children. Someone starts a song: When Israel was in Egypt's land. Others answer: let my people go. To the overseer on his horse, it might sound like an old Bible story. To the people singing, it was about them: Pharaoh, and chains, and a God who hears slaves and takes their side. Some of these songs carried hope. Some, people say, carried plans.
screen: `A FIELD BEFORE THE CIVIL WAR.` → `WHEN ISRAEL WAS IN EGYPT'S LAND.` → `A BIBLE STORY, OR THEIR STORY?`

segments.voice: A spiritual is a religious folk song made by enslaved Africans and their descendants in America. Their makers' names are mostly lost. They grew the way folk songs grow: sung, changed, passed on. Listen to what they chose: Moses and Pharaoh, the river Jordan, Daniel in the lions' den, the chariot coming for me. They took the Exodus and put themselves inside it. In the King James Bible, Moses and Aaron go in to Pharaoh and say: "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go." The spiritual made that line a refrain: "When Israel was in Egypt's land, Let my people go." Nobody needed to spell out who Pharaoh was. Now, the plans. Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery, wrote that when they sang about reaching Canaan, some of them meant the North. Harriet Tubman, who led people out of slavery, was called the Moses of her people, and an early biography says she used songs as signals. Historians are careful, though. Some famous claims, like songs that were secret maps, are hard to prove, and a few were written down only much later. The songs themselves show faith and resistance at once, with no need to choose. After the war, in 1871, a small group of students from Fisk University, a new school for freed people, went on tour to save it from debt. They sang spirituals for audiences who had never heard them sung like that, even for Queen Victoria. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried these songs to the world.
screen: `SONGS WITH NO KNOWN AUTHOR.` · `THEY PUT THEMSELVES IN EXODUS.` · `HOPE, AND SOMETIMES PLANS.` · `FISK, 1871: SONGS TO THE WORLD.` · then, large: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one spiritual, even a scrap, Go down, Moses, Swing low, sweet chariot, Wade in the water, Deep river, and hum it if it comes, or just remember its shape. Think of who first sang it: people with every reason to despair, singing about a God who sets slaves free. If you pray, hold in prayer anyone who is not free today; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
Spiritual. A song of faith made by enslaved Africans in America, full of Moses, Jordan and freedom.
Your line: let my people go. Exodus first, then theirs. Day one hundred thirty-seven, done.

any slow hymn sung softly at a church service

138.title: Holy, holy, holy
138.hook: Orthodox churches sing Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us
138.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians sing the Trisagion in the Divine Liturgy and pray it three times at the start of daily prayers, often making the sign of the cross each time; Catholics sing it on Good Friday, and many churches sing Isaiah's 'Holy, holy, holy' at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spiritual, songs of Moses and freedom, and your line: let my people go. Today, a far older chant.

Sunday morning in an Orthodox church. Candles, icons, incense hanging in the air, and often no pews, just people standing. At a certain point the choir begins a short chant, and the whole church seems to lean into it. Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. Then again. And again. Three times, sometimes more, slow enough that the words have room. It's short enough to learn on the way home, and its roots go back to a prophet's vision in the Temple.
screen: `CANDLES, ICONS, INCENSE.` → `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.` → `THREE TIMES, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Trisagion: Greek tris, three times, and hagion, holy. The thrice-holy. In the year King Uzziah died, the prophet Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, and creatures called seraphim calling to one another. In the King James Bible: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Why three times? Some readers hear Hebrew emphasis: say a word twice and it grows stronger; say it three times and there's nothing left to add. Holy beyond everything. At the end of the Bible, in Revelation, the song is still going: creatures around the throne "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." The Trisagion turns that cry into three lines people can pray, Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, then one very human request: have mercy on us. Nobody knows for certain who first put it together. A story people tell, from Constantinople in the fifth century, has an earthquake, and a boy caught up into the sky who heard angels singing it. What the records do show is bishops crying it out at the Council of Chalcedon, in 451. Orthodox churches sing it at the Divine Liturgy, and Orthodox prayer books open the daily prayers with it. Catholics sing it too, in Greek and Latin, on Good Friday. Other churches sing Isaiah's three holies in the communion service, the Sanctus, and in a nineteenth-century hymn that begins the same way. The pattern holds in all of them: first praise beyond words, then a plea for mercy, close to the ground.
screen: `TRIS, HAGION — THRICE HOLY.` · `ISAIAH SEES THE SERAPHIM.` · `THREE TIMES: HOLY BEYOND ALL.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN MERCY.` · then, large: `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand, whichever you like; in Orthodox churches, people often stand to pray. If you pray, say the Trisagion three times, slowly, one line per breath: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. If you don't, say the words as words and notice the shape, something vast, then something small asking for mercy, and after the third time, let the silence hold.
Trisagion. The thrice-holy. An ancient chant from Isaiah's vision: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.
Your line: close to the ground. Four short lines, short enough to carry home. Back tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 138 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GOSPEL, TAIZÉ AND WORSHIP SONGS.`

139.title: Gospel, Taizé and worship songs
139.hook: from Black gospel choirs to Taizé's repeated chants to modern worship bands
139.howItsDone: Christians sing in many styles: gospel choirs in many Black churches, Taizé chants at prayer services across denominations, contemporary worship bands in many Protestant churches, and unaccompanied chant in Orthodox and some Protestant churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trisagion, and your line: close to the ground. That closes a week of tithes, pastors and money, alms, a stranger's welcome and song.
screen: `CLOSE TO THE GROUND.` → `A WEEK OF GIVING AND SINGING.`

segments.voice: Three rooms, one Sunday. In the first, a choir in bright robes sways, a Hammond organ growls, and a soloist holds one note until the whole church is on its feet. In the second, a church in a French village, young people from many countries sit on the floor in candlelight, singing one short phrase over and over, quieter each time, until it feels like breathing. In the third, a converted warehouse, the lights go low, a drummer counts in, and a band plays while people raise their hands. Three sounds, and people in all three rooms might use the same word for it: prayer.
screen: `A CHOIR AND A HAMMOND ORGAN.` → `CANDLES AND ONE PHRASE, REPEATED.` → `A BAND IN A WAREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: Gospel means good news, and it names a music born in Black churches in America. It grew out of the spirituals, the blues and the energy of Pentecostal worship. The man often called its father is Thomas A. Dorsey, a Chicago blues pianist. His wife died giving birth, and their baby son soon after. In that grief, he sat down at a piano and wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord. Mahalia Jackson sang it across the world, and it was sung at Martin Luther King Junior's funeral. Gospel music often comes out of the hardest places. Taizé is something else: a small community of brothers in a village in France, begun by Brother Roger, its members from Protestant and Catholic churches. Young people come to spend a week there. The songs are short, one line of scripture or prayer sung again and again, in Latin or in many languages. The hope is that somewhere in the repeats, singers stop thinking about the words and start praying them. Then modern worship music: guitars, drums, songs sung straight to God, now familiar in churches around the world. Not every church uses instruments. Orthodox worship is traditionally sung without them, and some Protestant churches, like the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied on purpose. Others use every instrument they can find, because Psalm 150 says, in the King James Bible: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Christians argue about music, sometimes loudly. But a choir, a chant and a band can all carry the same prayer.
screen: `GOSPEL: BORN IN BLACK CHURCHES.` · `DORSEY: PRECIOUS LORD, OUT OF GRIEF.` · `TAIZÉ: ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `WITH INSTRUMENTS, OR WITHOUT.` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.`

segments.voice: In your mind, listen to the style of church music that feels least like you: the gospel choir, the quiet chant, the loud band, the old organ. Imagine yourself in that room, next to someone for whom this is exactly how prayer sounds, and let yourself be curious rather than critical. If you pray, pray alongside them in your mind.
Gospel. Good news, and a music born in Black churches in America, where grief and joy share one song.
Your line: every style can pray. That's a whole week of giving and singing, done.

140.title: Fellowship (Acts 2:42)
140.hook: the first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayers
140.carry: you weren't meant to do it alone
140.howItsDone: Many churches keep fellowship through shared meals, coffee after services, home groups and collections for people in need, and many Christians take Acts 2:42 as a picture of what church life should include.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gospel, Taizé and the worship band, and your line: every style can pray. A new week starts now: together and alone.
screen: `EVERY STYLE CAN PRAY.` → `A NEW WEEK: TOGETHER AND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem, a few weeks after Easter. Something has happened at Pentecost, and suddenly there are thousands of new believers where there were about a hundred and twenty. No church buildings. No clergy training. No plan. So what do they do, day to day? The book of Acts gives a snapshot, and it's surprisingly ordinary. They listen to the apostles teach. They eat together in each other's homes. They pray. They share what they have, so nobody goes without. It reads less like the founding of a religion than a very large family learning to live together. In the middle of that list sits a Greek word the church never stopped using.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF NEW BELIEVERS.` → `NO BUILDINGS, NO PLAN.` → `THEY ATE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Koinonia comes from koinos: common, shared, what belongs to everyone. Koinonia is having something in common: partnership, participation, sharing. English usually says fellowship, which is fine, but it's thicker than coffee after church. The verse, in the King James Bible: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayers. Churches still use that verse as a checklist. Elsewhere in the New Testament, Paul uses koinonia for money: a collection the churches took up for poor believers in Jerusalem. He uses it for the bread and cup: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" That word communion is koinonia. And he uses it for sharing in someone's suffering. One word covers a meal, a bank transfer, the Lord's Supper and a hard season. That tells you what the first Christians thought church was: not an event you attend, but a life you share. Acts says they ate their meals with gladness. Underneath it all sits a line from the very start of Genesis: "It is not good that the man should be alone." Some churches keep a meal after every service. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of the whole church, living and dead, sharing one communion. Many Protestants meet in homes midweek. Different forms, one conviction: faith was never meant to be carried solo.
screen: `KOINOS — COMMON, SHARED.` · `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYERS.` · `A MEAL, MONEY, THE CUP, SUFFERING.` · `A LIFE YOU SHARE.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT GOOD THAT THE MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: Picture the last meal you really shared with someone, not just ate near: where you were, what you talked about. Then let a face come to mind, someone you haven't eaten with in too long, a friend, a neighbor, a parent, someone who might be lonelier than they let on, and hold it for a minute. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
Koinonia. Greek for sharing a common life. Fellowship, communion, partnership: a meal, a purse and a faith held together.
Your line: you weren't meant to do it alone. That's one hundred forty days now.
